It is a time allotted by parliament for a very useful purpose. I am sorry to say that it is not always well attended by hon. members. However, it does afford members an excellent opportunity to put forward ideas and suggestions. I well remember as a backbencher how it provided a great opportunity to get the feel of the House. Many important measures have been passed by the House during private members' hour. For instance, the name Trans-Canada Air Lines was changed to Air Canada as the result of a private member's bill.
I remember speaking during private members' hour several years ago when bilingual cheques were introduced as the result of a private member's motion. I also had the privilege of putting forward a private member's resolution which brought about the parliamentary internship program which is now in its third year and has proven very satisfactory around Parliament Hill.
This bill on which I am about to speak deals with the public accounts committee. It is proposed as a reform measure to regularize the constitution and proceedings of that most important of committees, the public accounts committee. When speaking to this bill I would like to emphasize two very important principles. First, the executive should have no income which is not granted to it or otherwise sanctioned by parliament. Second, the executive should have no expenditures except those approved by parliament, in wages approved by parliament. The observation of these principles would be impossible were it not for the existence of a variety of rules, customs, devices and institutions. One of these institutions is the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, which is parliament's own auditing committee, responsible for scrutinizing the use or misuse of public funds.
Today, as the size and complexity of the federal government increase, the task of this committee grows more crucial if the principles of responsible government are to be safeguarded. By a year from now, March 31, 1974, the federal government, with more than 284,000 employees, will pay out roughly $10 billion for goods and services, and $6.5 billion in grants and contributions, along with supplementary estimates that are likely to come forward. This will mean a total expenditure of approximately $20 billion. It is the role of parliament, and of the public accounts committee in particular, to ensure that these
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
sums of money authorized by parliament annually are being utilized in the ways parliament intended.
Let us look at some of the weaknesses in the parliamentary control of public funds. In Canada, the different stages in the administrative process of public expenditures are laid down in the Financial Administration Act. Among other things, the act ensures the public accounts and the report of the Auditor General are laid before parliament each year. This is all set out by statute. What parliament does with the public accounts and the Auditor General's report is not laid down by any statute and depends entirely on custom and the business priorities ol the government. This has resulted in a weakening of parliament's control over public funds and in the increasing and unchallenged power of the executive. Furthermore, it has seriously reduced the effectiveness and efficiency of the public accounts committee.
The Canadian system of control of public expenditures, like any chain of command, is no stronger than its weakest link. The purpose of this bill is to strengthen the weakest link, namely, parliament's scrutiny of public funds. The House of Commons, through this committee, should be able to scrutinize thoroughly and without impediment the accounts of Canada and the annual report of the Auditor General, and present to the House for debate reports which empower the executive to take action, thereby completing the cycle of parliamentary control.
What are some of the weaknesses in the House rules? Under the Standing Orders, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts must be struck within a given time at the commencement of the first session of each parliament. Unlike the other committees of the House which must have the estimates referred to them, the public accounts committee may never be called or given an order of reference by the government should it not be in the interest of the government to do so. The executive does not have to organize the committee and does not have to refer anything to it.
May I give just a few examples of the delays that have occurred in the work of the public accounts committee. As you know, Mr. Speaker, it is up to the government House leader to call the organization meetings of all committees of the House, including the public accounts committee. In the twenty-sixth parliament, the opening was May 16, 1963, and the organization meeting of the public accounts committee was not held until October 16. In other words, six months elapsed before the committee was even organized. From the opening of the twenty-seventh parliament on January 18, 1966, to the organization meeting on March 1, 1966, two months elapsed. That was not so bad. From the opening of the twenty-eighth parliament on May 8, 1967, to the organization meeting on May 5, 1968, 12 months elapsed. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, a whole year went by before the public accounts committee was called for an organization meeting! From the opening of the twenty-ninth parliament, the present parliament, on January 4 of this year, to the organization meeting on March 14, two and a half months elapsed.
What about the reference of work to the public accounts committee? From the opening of the twenty-sixth parliament on May 16, 1963, to the first reference in May, 1964, a
April 6, 1973

year elapsed. From the opening of the second session of the twenty-seventh parliament on May 8, to the first reference to the committee, several months elapsed. The present parliament opened on January 4 and there has been no reference of any work to the public accounts committee since then. Three months have elapsed. Yet that committee is behind in its work; it has not yet finished the 1971 report of the Auditor General. The Auditor General's report for 1968 was tabled on March 16, 1969, and was referred to the committee on April 16, 1969. Only one month elapsed. Only the first volume of the 1969 report was referred to the committee. Apparently, from the records that I have been able to locate, the second volume was never referred to the committee.
The Auditor General's 1970 report was tabled on June 4, 1971, and was referred to the committee on September 22 of the same year. So there is still delay between the time the Auditor General tables his report and when it is referred to the committee. I will refer to these delays later in my speech. This practice has weakened parliament's responsibility as the guardian of the public purse and, furthermore, the responsibility of the public accounts committee to examine critically public expenditures.
Under the present rules, committee reports may be presented to the House by committee chairmen. They may be concurred in and debated. It is very seldom done, but they could be. It has been the experience of the public accounts committee that its reports have been tabled with little or no debate. This may be the result of the committee's limited power to secure orders of reference and government recognition.
The committee has no power to enforce the implementation of its own recommendations; it is entirely dependent upon the will of the executive. In Britain, the treasury has the responsibility of reporting to the public accounts committee the status of outstanding recommendations and their effective implementation. The Treasury Board of Canada does not have this responsibility unless directed by the cabinet. There are some other limitations. Attendance and participation at committee meetings pose problems for members with many parliamentary commitments and, in turn, the detailed attention they can give to the committee's inquiries. There is a growing need for research assistance and professional services to facilitate the committee in its work.
What are the solutions? There are two or three possible ways of dealing with the problems. First, amend the statute, the Financial Administration Act; second, amend the Standing Orders of the House of Commons; third, deal with the problems by a separate bill or an act. I have chosen to introduce a bill, but it is immaterial to me how the change is brought about, Mr. Speaker.
I know that the Australian government has had a committee of public accounts act since 1913 and it has worked very well. I have had the opportunity of visiting the standing committee on public accounts in Australia and talking with the chairman and secretary. I also have had the privilege of sitting in at a meeting of the United Kingdom public accounts committee. Both these committees work and are organized under a statute. Unlike Australia, the
Public Accounts Committee
public accounts committee in Britain receives its authority from a specific British House of Commons standing order No. 86. In both Australia and Great Britain the public accounts committee has specific terms of reference. The Canadian committee, on the other hand, observes the general terms contained in the Standing Orders along with other standing committees of the House. They are just general terms.
What are my recommendations, Mr. Speaker? The purpose of Bill C-19 is to ensure that the responsibilities traditionally handed down to the public accounts committee are safeguarded by statute. Presently they are not. They should be. Therefore, it is recommended that the bill include the following four main points: first, the public accounts committee personnel shall automatically be chosen and organized during the first 15 working days of each session of parliament. The Standing Orders of the House set out that the members must be chosen at the commencement of each session, but there is nothing to say that an organization meeting must be held. As I have proven by dates, we have had lapses of up to a year between the day the members were chosen and the organization meeting was held.
Second, the chairman of that committee, unlike the chairman of other parliamentary committees, shall not be a member of the party forming the government, but shall be a member of the official opposition. This is the system we have at the present time but there is nothing in the statute to say it should be that way. In the Australian and British systems it is laid down by statute. Third, the public accounts of income and expenditure, and the Auditor General's report shall automatically be referred to the public accounts committee as soon as they are tabled in the House, and not be delayed from such reference and study at the whim of the government of the day. I am looking at this in a non-partisan way. I am looking at it as a long-term statute for this parliament of Canada, no matter what party is in power. I feel that these principles should all be laid down by statute and there should not be as much power given to the executive as there is at the present time.
Fourth, all recommendations made by the public accounts committee to parliament shall be reported on annually, or sooner, by the responsible minister upon action taken by him or the Treasury Board. This would make it compulsory that the recommendations made by the committee should be handled and reported within a year. I do not care which method is used, Mr. Speaker, whether it is the Financial Administration Act, Standing Orders of the House of Commons or a separate bill. One thing I do know, however, is that if the public accounts committee is to perform the function it was meant to perform, it should be independent of the executive and set up by statute as it is in Australia and the United Kingdom.
I hope my bill is not talked out, but if there is a feeling that there should be more discussion on it, I will agree to whatever the House decides. I should like to have it referred to the finance committee or the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, however, so that they could decide which form the statute should take.
It is very important, as I see it, that in the years that lie ahead we should follow the proven and tested system

April 6, 1973
Public Accounts Committee
which other countries have used. We are operating under a sort of hearsay operation, a sort of tradition. There is nothing laid down by statute, and I sincerely feel there should be. It was with that line of thought that I introduced Bill C-19.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' PUBLIC BILLS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT (PUBLIC ACCOUNTS) MEASURE TO REGULARIZE CONSTITUTION AND PROCEEDINGS OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to make my modest contribution to the study of Bill-19 to amend the Financial Administration Act (Public Accounts) introduced by my excellent friend the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales). The hon. member guided my first steps in the House and in the Public Accounts Committee after my first election in 1970. We became friends through this association and I have had the privilege of visiting Guelph the splendid city of his birth. I hold the hon. member in high esteem. I should like to tell him that I sympathise with his complaints and his desire to find some way to accelerate the proceedings of the committee, to alter or reform it and make it more efficient in order to be able to study various public account items and the report of the Auditor General with greater care and attention than at present. In my opinion, that bill is precisely meant to make the committee more efficient. Several reasons have been put forward by my colleague, the sponsor of the bill, to explain why the proceedings of the committee are not carried out as quickly as expected.
He broached a few points, and if I am allowed to do so, I would like to state a few reasons why the proceedings of that committee have often been delayed. While I do not have his experience as a member of that committee, I wish just the same to give some information. I wish to point out in the first place the delayed tabling of the Auditor General's report whose consideration is the main item in the order of reference from the House. And that report-as stipulated in the statutes- must be tabled fifteen days after parliament reconvenes or the beginning of a session. And three months and a half will soon have elapsed since Parliament reconvened and as we know, that report has not been tabled yet. And this is the sixth year, if I remember correctly, that we are unable to get that report.
The Auditor General has been saying every year since I became a member of that committee that for all kinds of reasons, it was hard for him to hire staff, that the government, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and many other things were to blame, but never his incompetence or his inability to get the necessary staff, since it is up to him to recruit the staff he needs to discharge his duties.
While discussing the matter with some of his colleagues who have left and others who are still serving under him, several gave a few reasons to explain the delay in tabling the report or the difficulties experienced by the Auditor General in getting and keeping a staff.
Of course, in a service like his, as in any other organization, there is a certain percentage of the staff that cannot practically be retained, while in a private enterprise of a similar nature, if after five years business is successful and one has been able to keep 50 per cent of his staff, it means that he is a good boss and that the staff is well

paid. On the other hand, in the public service, I am told that the staff stability rate is much higer than in the Auditor General's office. There are surely reasons for this. As a matter of fact, we examined the different reasons that were given by various people in connection with this position and it was said that the employees did not enjoy the same job security as those in the public service because they were operating within a very restricted perimeter. The staff numbers perhaps 200 at best. The public service has thousands of civil servants on its payroll and so offers much more opportunities to those with ambition.
Recruiting opportunities have never been rejected. Each year all the budgets introduced were examined and never submitted to amendments or restrictions. If the Auditor General was requesting additional credits to hire personnel he was never refused and was thus able to ensure the renewal and training of his personnel and his department was as efficient as the House and the government were entitled to expect it to be and because this department should operate as well as all the other federal bodies.
In my opinion this explains why committee business has often been delayed. This most serious reason explains why the report is tabled late each year.
I have a few other reservations about the bill, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to deal with them. I should like, first, to mention that this statutory authority perhaps may be desirable but I am surprised at the choice my colleague made, namely, the Financial Administration Act. His proposal is most surprising, since the Auditor General is a servant of parliament and should not be appointed under legislation generally administered by the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board. I also looked into the Australian arrangement and have found that the public accounts committee in Australia is a joint committee; it is composed of members of the Senate and members of the House of Commons. On the other hand, our public accounts committee is composed solely of members of the House of Commons.
The bill also provides for the chairman to be a member of the opposition. This practice has been followed in our committee but it is not a matter of statute; it is a matter of convention. It has always been so. It is our tradition that the chairman of the public accounts committee shall be a member of the official opposition party. I agree with this convention. It is a good one and we have the good fortune of having an excellent chairman, as I said at the beginning of my remarks.
I have other concerns respecting the proposed bill and I should like to deal with them. One of my concerns relates to the powers conferred on this committee and the provisions set out in proposed sections 55G to 55S. I believe it might be extremely prejudicial to the ordinarily understood constitutional position of ministers with respect to parliament to insert in this statute authority which might be interpreted as requiring a minister to appear and produce documents. I should like, as well, to draw attention to the effect of conferring the powers in question on a committee of the House, since the result may be that we
April 6, 1973

should confer on such a committee greater power than that possessed by parliament itself. Indeed, if any thought is given to proceeding with this legislation, I would suggest that it be referred formally to the Department of Justice so that they may have a look at the implications and various aspects of the bill.
After providing for the establishment of the committee, there are in the bill just two sections dealing with the duties of the committee and its modus operandi through subcommittees. Following that, the greater part of the proposed legislation deals with procedures for taking evidence, offences and penalties. The provisions for offences and penalties are not consistent with section 92, the section of the Financial Administration Act which deals with offences and penalties.
I should now like to deal with section 55E(l)(c), which speaks of the form of "the public accounts or in the method of keeping them". This is Australian wording and, within the context of the Financial Administration Act, creates a failure to differentiate between the accounts of Canada and the public accounts. In section 55E(2), where the words "shall report annually or sooner if he desires" appear, since the word "annually" covers a period of time rather than a fixed point in time, the word "sooner" would need to be replaced by a word or expression such as "more frequently". This particular subsection does not appear in the Australian legislation, I might add. Further, in section 55E(2) the words "Minister responsible for that department" would need to be replaced by the words "appropriate minister", the approved terminology of the Financial Administration Act.
I should also like to refer to section 55Q, which is intended as an authority for expenditures. Except for the last six words, the section is taken from the Australian act and would not appear to be an appropriate matter for a private member's bill under Canadian parliamentary practice. I suppose this is realized, Mr. Speaker. Of course, there may be many more reasons why we should improve the operation of this committee. Perhaps we should find a way of changing the whole parliamentary system; but that is another problem.

I will be very brief in my remarks, Mr. Speaker. In a very few words, this bill can be described as one which seeks to add independence and power to the work of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. That means adding power for the good work of that committee, on behalf of parliament and the public, in which it is engaged whenever it has the opportunity to block the loopholes through which many millions of dollars have escaped in unproductive expenditures-in other words, waste.
The hon. member who introduced this bill knows very well whereof he speaks. As has been indicated, he has been and, hopefully, will continue to be chairman of the
Public Accounts Committee
Standing Committee on Public Accounts. He is an excellent chairman in every respect. I think he adds to his excellency in that capacity by the bill he has introduced.

speechtext:
As the hon. member for Wellington suggested, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts is one of the most important committees of parliament. It deals with the public's money and tries to make the best use of the money provided by the public through taxes. I think the hon. member for Wellington and others will agree that, at best, we are being guided through the labrynth of ever expanding governmental responsibilities and expenditures by the Auditor General, on one hand, and the chairman of our committee on the other.
While engaged in very important work, the committee can hardly do justice to the very important financial matters that come before it. What we are doing in that committee as it is presently constituted, and with the limited powers it has, is touching the peak of the iceberg of public expenditures. It is a multibillion dollar iceberg. We are doing our best, with the aid of the Auditor General and his officials, to probe the tip of that iceberg.
I believe the committee would benefit by the proposals put forward by the hon. member. The committee is in a very strategic position. It could do more, with a little more independence, to effect great savings and make better use of the public's money. I support in particular the proposal in this bill which calls upon Treasury Board to require a report, at its disposition, of the anti-waste recommendations of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts within a reasonable time. At present, after many hearings and doing as well as we can, we make recommendations some of which go unanswered or are hardly acknowledged and certainly are not put into effect for years. This is a waste of public money. If Treasury Board were required to prepare a report, at its disposition, on what action the different departments have taken on the recommendations of the public accounts committee, this would be an excellent step forward.
There are one or two other points which would be of benefit to the committee and parliament if they were adopted or considered in line with this bill. The public accounts committee should have a permanent secretary to improve the continuity of its work. The committee is faced with many detailed and complex financial matters. It should have the benefit of at least two qualified research people to help in its deliberations. I agree with the hon. member who introduced this bill that it would be most beneficial to have the government, through Treasury Board, acknowledge the recommendations of the committee and their disposition.
I do not want to take much more time. I would like to see this bill sent to the appropriate committee for consideration and action. To strengthen the public accounts committee and help it to do better work is not sufficient. I believe that at least every ten years there should be an in-depth and in-breadth investigation of the structure of the Canadian government and its responsibilities and ever growing expenditures. I believe the last such investigation was carried out ten years ago. In view of the great expansion of government expenditures within the last ten years,

April 6, 1973
Public Accounts Committee
the time is ripe for an in-depth and in-breadth examination of the whole structure of the functions of the government and the spending of public money.
This would do more to probe the tip of the iceberg, which is important enough and which is really the function as the committee is presently constituted, which the public accounts committee carries out. We need something more basic. We need to examine the continuing waste of public money as well as the consequences of it. I take rny seat in the hope that the bill will proceed to a committee for action.

Mr. ].-Roland Comtois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance): Mr. SpeaKer, I should like to say a few words on Bill C-19, entitled an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act and deal more particularly with the Public Accounts Committee its constitution and the procedure it should follow.
I believe that all the speakers have recognized the importance of that committee, whose duties are to supervise and scrutinize government expenses, besides analysing as minutely as possible the Auditor General's report.
The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) recommends the adoption of this bill after consideration in the House. At the same time he points out how weak parliamentary control over government expenses is. I must say that even if that control can appear weak from, many standpoints, it is nevertheless essential to the operation of any democracy. My colleague the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) has dealt at some length with the matter of the Auditor General's annual report, which is almost always tabled late, and this under all sorts of pretences. Now, I would hope that with a new Auditor General, new rules and a new legislation on the operation of the public accounts committee, we might in the near future get those reports on time, so that we may analyze and study them and make the necessary recommendations each year.
The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) has suggested that the Treasury Board report on the results obtained following the changes introduced as a consequence of the inquiries conducted by the Auditor General in the discharge of his duties. I believe that this is a very good idea which the house should perhaps consider. As to his suggestion that we secure the services of a permanent staff, especially those of a secretary and qualified research personnel, I believe that it is a wise one which could contribute to immensely improve the work of the committee.
It might also be good for members of the committee themselves to be as permanent, if possible, at least for the scan of a parliament.
The mover of Bill C-19 wants to strengthen the power of the committee to scrutinize government expenditures and in fact it all boils down to strengthening the power of Parliament to scrutinize government expenditures. The purpose of the bill is good: the hon. member pointed out several weaknesses in the operation of that committee. For example, he talked about the delays in establishing the committee and he went back to the 25th Parliament but I think that if he had gone further back he would have

found the same delays that we have today and which can be due to a host of circumstances beyond the control of either the government or parliament.
Evidently, we are having difficulties due sometimes to a host of circumstances in all committees and I wonder if it is need for special legislation or if by simply reviewing the procedure we could not reach the same result.
Mention has been made of committee chairmen who by tradition in Canada are members of the opposition. It is obvious that it is not in the books but I think that precedents and traditions in our parliamentary system will always be respected. I think that budget estimates and public accounts should be referred as sson as possible to the committee for examination as well as the report of the Auditor General which, hopefully, in the future will be submitted within a prescribed time limit.
There is often concern about the fact that the recom-mandations of the Committee on Public Accounts are not taken into consideration by the government and that there are delays perhaps more or less warranted before immediate action is taken. I think that there is good understanding within the committee. I have had the pleasure to sit on it on several occasions; I think in spite of everything that can be said that it is one of the committees with the best records and who is doing an excellent job, although there are obviously some difficulties. In spite of that, I think all the committee members would agree that the chairman, whom I have known since I have been a Member of Parliament, is doing an excellent job and deserves the congratulations of all his colleagues. As was pointed out earlier, the hon. member for Wellington will remain chairman of the committee on public accounts for as long as he is a Member of Parliament and of the opposition.
I should like to end my remarks by saying that it is obvious that the more independent a committee, the more independent his members and the better the work done, bearing in mind the political context in which we live. In this committee especially, most of the time there is an absence of partisanship that makes me hope that in spite of all the difficulties and disadvantages that is has to face, the committee on public accounts will continue to do the work expected of it to the satisfaction, I would think, of the large majority of members.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' PUBLIC BILLS
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT (PUBLIC ACCOUNTS) MEASURE TO REGULARIZE CONSTITUTION AND PROCEEDINGS OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for; Wellington (Mr. Hales) for bringing this measure before us. The functioning of the standing committees of the House of Commons has been engaging our attention for some time. Indeed, it would seem that the whole committee system is under attack at the present time, since it is trying to operate under circumstances which were not envisaged. Consequently, we are discovering that there are imperfections in our rules giving rise to difficulties which will probably have to be fought out on the floor of this chamber.
The problem is self-evident and it is one which will not be easily resolved. It is one which I hope will be discussed
April 6, 1973

in detail in the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. At the present time, this committee is engaged in studying the estimates of the House of Commons but, hopefully, when these have been dealt with it will turn to the larger question of the rules governing these committees and the way in which they relate to the House of Commons.
I wish to say a few words on the proposition the hon. member for Wellington has advanced. It has to do not only with the public accounts committee; it seems to involve the relationship of the Auditor General with the House of Commons and parliament in general as well as the question of the appointment of a new Auditor General. Hon. members will no doubt recall that a number of proposals have been put forward as part of a possible new legislative enactment to govern the activities of the Auditor General. A recommendation was put forward some time ago by the public accounts committee itself. It was not acceptable to the House of Commons and so far we have not been able to resolve this dilemma. It would seem to me, however, that the new Auditor General might make recommendations acceptable both to the public accounts committee and to the House of Commons. For this reason I believe the period following the appointment of the new Auditor General would be a much more suitable time at which to legislate the responsibilities in question.
The Financial Administration Act is not a particularly suitable vehicle for this purpose since it deals with the financial responsibilities of Crown corporations and other federal agencies. If we were to insert artificially a description of the role and functions of the public accounts committee, I believe we would be stretching the scope of the act somewhat too far. Indeed, we would be guilty of a crime with which the government was accused last session, that of trying to insert too many pieces of legislation under the title of one bill. I have in mind omnibus bills which the government introduced in past sessions. Hopefully, this practice will not be continued.
I want to draw the attention of hon. members to the delicacy with which we must approach this question. Although the successor to the former Auditor General has been named, he will not assume his duties until some time in July. In the meantime his position is being filled by the Assistant Auditor General. Consequently, it seems to me that until the new Auditor General has had an opportunity to look into his new responsibilities and to read the past minutes of the public accounts committee when the Auditor General's Act was discussed, and indeed to read this debate, it would be somewhat presumptuous of us to give second reading to this proposal and send it to a committee for discussion before the new Auditor General had taken up his position. It seems to me that the least we can do in these circumstances in which we are in transit from one Auditor General to another is to display the courtesy of waiting for him to take control of that position and to make recommendations to the public accounts committee.
I feel it would be far better for the Auditor General to make recommendations to the public accounts committee and for the committee, as a result of studies it has engaged in over the past several years, to make recommendations to this House. I recognize, as I am sure other
Public Accounts Committee
hon. members do, that this transfer is an onerous one. I think in all justice, also, that hon. members will recognize that the position of Auditor General is a matter of some contention between various parties in the House of Commons.
It may well be that even an act of parliament on the Auditor General written in God's own hand would not be acceptable to hon. members of the House. It does seem to me that until we have reached a reasonable agreement in the House of Commons as to the development of the Auditor General's position under an Auditor General's act, we would be presumptuous in moving forward with this proposal. What I am suggesting is that we should not move forward on a piecemeal basis, but instead should march forward with a co-ordinated and logical approach to the whole problem.
The dilemma hon. members have in coping with the estimates of the government is illustrated most profusely in the way in which committee activities have taken place this year. Hon. members know that the entire estimates of the government are referred to standing committees and that these standing committees have until the end of May to complete their detailed study of the estimates. The Standing Committee on Public Accounts finds itself in a different role. It is designed to receive and report upon the findings of the Auditor General. The role of this standing committee could be competitive but it is designed to be co-ordinative and co-operative.
Our dilemma, as a result of the committee system at the present time, is that Members of Parliament find it takes a great deal of time to carry out the work which has to be done in criticizing the spending of the government in a detailed and precise way. It strikes me that this is not the fault of the structure of the committee system as it now stands but is a problem of the individual member of parliament. We often hear in the House of Commons that there is no time for the House to properly and seriously examine governmental spending. In point of fact, there is ample time under our present system, having regard to the supply motion, allocated days and the time allotted for specific examination under other motions.
Your Honour will note that this is not the approach hon. Members of Parliament take. Very seldom do they come forward with detailed plans to eliminate government spending. Instead, the general tenor of the debates since the last election has been for the government to extend its spending in a whole series of trends; in respect of increased pensions to senior citizens and veterans, increased welfare payments, increased subsidies to farmers and corporations, and increased payments for education. The House of Commons is never free of requests for increased governmental expenditures. However, the real skinflint of the parliamentary system is not the opposition, not the members of the government backbenchers and not the members of the small parties; the actual skinflint is the Minister of Finance and the cabinet, not individual members seeking to have the government increase spending programs.
Your Honour has properly drawn to the attention of the House of Commons the fact that in the third report of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development it is suggested the government make grants

Public Accounts Committee
to the Native Council of Canada, I believe it is to provide proper research facilities to examine aboriginal claims. I am sure that members of the House of Commons will agree that this is a laudable aim. However, there is a procedural point in respect of whether a committee of the House can recommend to the House of Commons an expenditure of money without royal recommendation or the recommendation of a minister. This is a very serious procedural point and I give notice that when such motions are brought forward, some hon. members on this side will argue it.
The point 1 am trying to make is that not only do members make such recommendations in the normal course of their duties; they seek out opportunities which,
in my opinion, are clearly not allowed by the rules, and continually importune the House of Commons to authorize further expenditures. Each member comes to the House of Commons with ideas that are perfectly sensible, reasonable and logical. Very few members come here to suggest that we must cut back expenditures in respect of specific items or departments. The problem, therefore, has become one of tradition in the House of Commons. The idea of cutting expenditures has evaporated and now we are continually seeking increased expenditures.
